lines.content: Shared instructions for AI coding agents working on this CS2103T team project (tP).
All team members use this file, so keep it short and team-wide.
Read [Maintaining this file](#maintaining-this-file) before you edit it.
* Brownfield evolution of AddressBook-Level3 (AB3). Contact management stays the primary focus.
* Base package: `seedu.address`. Layers: `ui`, `logic`, `model`, `storage`, `commons`. See `docs/DeveloperGuide.md` for the architecture.

* Follow the current course website (`nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1`). Past semesters' sites, such as `nus-cs2103-ay2526s1`, describe rules that no longer apply, such as the PE dry run and `Appendix: Planned Enhancements`.

Features are frozen. The work now is fixing leftover bugs, tightening error messages, and cleaning up the UG, DG, and UML diagrams. Source: [week 12 tP tasks](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/schedule/week12/project.html).
* Dates: the freeze started Fri 30 Oct 2026, 10:00. Final deliverables are due Tue 3 Nov 2026, 14:00 (14:00:01 is late). Push no code for 30 days after that. The PE runs Fri 6 Nov to Sat 7 Nov.
* The UG and DG are submitted through the team repo. A commit pushed after the deadline is late, even if it was made before the deadline.

* When drafting PE bug responses, assign each bug to the member who owns the feature. Unassigned bugs beyond a set limit, and wrong rejections, downgrades, or objections, cost marks. Source: [PE](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-pe.html).
* Do not add commands, prefixes, parameters, or other features. If a fix seems to need one, stop and ask the user.

* Each member may change at most 15% or 150 lines (whichever is higher) of their own `src/main` code during v1.6. Blank lines and comments count. Going over costs at least 2 marks. Tests, docs, and diagrams have no limit.
* Lines you edit count against your quota, even lines a teammate wrote. Refactoring counts too.
* Before you change `src/main`, weigh the fix against its line cost and regression risk. Make the smallest change that fixes the bug.
* In the handoff, report the branch's `src/main` changes from `git diff --stat $(git merge-base upstream/master HEAD) -- src/main`. Members track their running total on the tP Code Dashboard.
* Triage each bug before you touch code:
1. Should have been fixed in v1.5: fix it now. If the fix costs too many lines, state the limitation in the UG instead.

1. Worth fixing only in a later version: leave the code, and list it under **Known issues** in the UG if users are likely to hit it. Say that it is planned for a future version, so the team can respond `NotInScope` to a PE report. This lowers the severity of a PE report but does not cancel it. Do not add an `Appendix: Planned Enhancements` to the DG; it no longer protects against PE reports.
1. Intended behavior: leave the code, and make sure the UG states the behavior.
A private tutor who teaches secondary school students (levels S1 to S5) in Singapore and prefers typing commands to using a mouse.
* Tutors many students across different schools, levels, and subjects, and takes on new students from their first enquiry.
* Contacts both students and their guardians, and often needs to find a student quickly while a guardian is on the phone.
* Keeps notes on each student, such as strong and weak topics, test scores, and reminders, to tailor lessons.
* Needs to see one student's full record on one screen before a lesson, and to group students by school, level, or subject when planning.
Value proposition: keep every student's contacts, guardian contacts, school, level, subjects, and lesson notes in one place, and reach any of it with a short typed command.

Design every feature for this user. When a choice affects what users can enter, check it against [Preventing bugs and feature flaws](#preventing-bugs-and-feature-flaws). For example, Singapore names often contain `s/o` or `d/o`.
* `./gradlew check`: compile, run checkstyle, and run all tests. Must pass before you commit.
* `cd .github && ./run-checks.sh`: check trailing whitespace, missing EOF newlines, and CRLF line endings.
* CI runs `./gradlew check coverage` on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows.
CI must pass on all three platforms before a change is ready to push. Run what CI runs:
1. `./gradlew clean check coverage` from the repo root.
1. Confirm coverage is still 50% or higher. See [Tests](#tests).
1. `git status` and `git diff`: confirm the change contains only what the task needs.
Code that passes on your machine can still fail CI on another OS:
* Build file paths with `Path.of(...)` or `Path.resolve(...)`, never by joining strings with `/` or `\`.
* Do not hard-code `\n` when comparing multi-line output in tests; use `System.lineSeparator()`.
* Do not rely on file name case. Windows and macOS treat `Person.java` and `person.java` as the same file.
* Do not edit the Gradle wrapper files. CI validates the wrapper.
If a check fails, fix the cause. Do not delete tests, add `@Disabled`, add `CHECKSTYLE.OFF` comments, or edit `config/checkstyle/` to make it pass unless the user asks.
Never violate these. They come from the [tP constraints](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-constraints.html).
* Typed commands are the primary input. The GUI gives feedback; it does not replace the CLI.
* Single user. No shared data files and no multi-user features.
* Store data locally in human-editable text files (JSON, like AB3). No DBMS.
* Must run on Windows, Linux, and macOS with only Java 25 installed. No OS-specific libraries or paths.
* No installer, no remote server of our own, and one JAR under 100 MB that runs on every OS, including macOS on ARM and Windows WSL.
* Read and write files only in the folder that contains the JAR and its subfolders. Never change OS settings.
* Third-party libraries must be free, open source, permissively licensed, and approved by the teaching team first. Do not add dependencies without asking the user.
* GUI must work at 1920x1080 (100% and 125% scale) and stay usable at 1280x720 (150% scale).
* Every commit leaves the product working. Deliver in small increments.
The [se-edu Java coding standard (intermediate)](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html) is a graded component, not a suggestion.
Checkstyle (`config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml`) catches layout, braces, whitespace, import order, and missing Javadoc.
It does not catch the rules below, so apply them yourself:
* Booleans start with `is`, `has`, `was`, `can`, or similar: `isDone`, `hasTag()`, `setDone(boolean isDone)`.
* Methods are verbs; classes are nouns.
* Acronyms are not all caps: `exportHtml()`, not `exportHTML()`.
* Scope decides name length: loop indices may be `i`, `j`; wide-scope names are descriptive.
* Group related constants with a shared prefix: `COLOR_RED`, `COLOR_BLUE`.
* Declare variables in the smallest scope and initialize them at declaration.
* Fields are never public, except `public final` fields in pure data classes.
Rules checkstyle does enforce, for reference while writing code:
* 4-space indent, no tabs. Wrapped lines indent 8 spaces. Lines stay at 110 characters or fewer; 120 is the hard limit.
* K&R braces. Always use braces for `if`, `else`, `for`, and `while` bodies.
* `switch`: indent `case` labels; every `switch` has a `default`; mark intentional fall-through with `// Fallthrough`.
* Break wrapped lines after commas and before operators (including `.`). Keep `=` at the end of the line.
* Imports: no wildcards. Order: static imports, then `java`/`javax`, then `org`, then everything else (`javafx`, `seedu`). Alphabetical within each group, with a blank line between groups.
* Every public class and every public method needs a header comment. Getters, setters, and `@Override` methods whose parent Javadoc applies are exempt.
* Start the summary with a third-person verb: "Returns ...", "Adds ...".
* Put a blank line between the description and the tags.
* Use `@param` for all parameters or none. End each tag description with a period.
* Returns the person at the given index in the filtered list.
* @param index Zero-based index of the person.
* Mirror the `src/main` package structure under `src/test`. Reuse builders and typical data in `seedu.address.testutil`.
* Keep JUnit test coverage at 50% or higher. Prioritize the code where a bug would hurt most, such as parsers, commands, and the model.
* Before you add JUnit test cases, list the cases you plan to add and ask the user to confirm.
* Add or update tests with every behavior change. Cover the cases in the [test checklist](#test-checklist).

* When you add or change behavior, also review the existing tests for that code. Update tests that still expect the old behavior, and make sure the tests would fail if a later change broke the new behavior.

* `./gradlew coverage` only writes the JaCoCo report to `build/reports/jacoco/coverage/html/index.html`. The build does not fail when coverage drops below 50%, so open the report and check the **Total** row yourself.
Code quality is graded along with the coding standard. Checkstyle does not check any of these.
* Keep methods short. Aim for under about 30 lines; extract a well-named helper when a method grows past that.
* Avoid deep nesting. Use guard clauses and return early so the happy path stays at the lowest indent level.
* Keep one level of abstraction per method. A method either coordinates steps or does low-level work, not both.
* Split complicated expressions into named intermediate variables.
* Replace magic numbers and strings with named constants: `MAX_TAG_LENGTH`, not `50`.
* Do not reuse a variable for a second purpose.
* Remove duplicated logic by extracting it, not by copy-pasting and tweaking.
* Delete dead code. Do not leave it commented out.
* Never leave a `catch` block empty. Handle the exception, or log it and explain why ignoring it is safe.
* Keep it simple. Do not optimize before there is a measured need.
* Comment what and why, not how. Do not restate what the code already says.
Other teams will test this app and file bugs against it, and every accepted bug costs marks, including bugs inherited from AB3.
Treat this section as correctness requirements, not polish.
Define "correct" from the user's point of view, not from what is easy to parse or store.
Deliberate sabotage, such as typing a 30-digit phone number on purpose, is not a bug.
A plausible mistake is: a missing space between parameters, a repeated prefix, an extra space, an empty value, or extra parameters or text where the command expects none.
A plausible mistake must never crash the app, corrupt the data file, or leave the app unusable.
* Do: `add n/John Doep/98765432` shows the name rule and a hint to check for a missing space before a prefix.
* Do: `list 5` and `delete 1 2` show an error instead of ignoring the extra text.
* Don't: let the value flow through and fail later with an uncaught exception.
* Do: `delete 99999999999` shows an invalid index error.
* Don't: call `Integer.parseInt` without handling overflow. Numbers from user input follow the same rule as any other mistake.
Define "valid" by what real users need to enter, not by the narrowest data type.
* Limits must be reasonable for the target user.
* Don't: pick a limit that real users hit without saying so.
* Do: when a rule is narrow on purpose, state it exactly in the UG and say why.
* Do: pick a limit no realistic value reaches, and document it in the UG.
* Do not reject symbols that real values contain.

* Names accept only ASCII letters, digits, and spaces (`Name.VALIDATION_REGEX`), so `Rajesh s/o Kumar`, `Mary-Jane O'Brien`, and `J. Tan` are rejected. The UG and DG document this choice, but testers may still report it as a feature flaw. Do not change the rule without asking the user.
* Do: when a symbol is hard to parse, improve the parser before banning the symbol.
* Warn rather than block unusual but harmless input.
* Don't: reject `+65 9123 4567`, `9123-4567` or an overseas number. `ParserUtil.parsePhone` removes spaces, dashes, and a leading `+65` when the rest is a Singapore number.
* Do: save a number that isn't a Singapore number and add a warning with `CommandResult.withWarning`, as `add` and `edit` do for `p/` and `gp/`.
* Still guard against harmful input. Accepting a value that makes data ambiguous or breaks a later command is also a flaw. Block it or warn about it.
* Don't: let a 100-character name push other fields off screen, or cut it so only the first few characters show.
* Do: wrap long text so the user can read the whole value. Check it at 1280x720.
Error messages are the riskiest text in the app. Testers trigger every one, and a vague, wrong, or inconsistent message is a bug.
* Name the field and the rule the value broke.
* Don't: "Invalid input." or "Invalid command format!" for a single bad field.
* Do: "Email `john@` is missing a domain after `@`."
* Keep messages short and plain: one or two sentences, everyday words, no exclamation marks.
* Do not guess what the user meant. A guess that is wrong misleads the user. When a value could have failed for more than one reason, state the rule broadly and briefly instead of naming one cause.
* Don't: "Did you mean `S3`?" or a hint that assumes which mistake the user made.
* Don't: swing the other way and list every sub-rule. `Email.MESSAGE_CONSTRAINTS` is a numbered list today; treat it as a known flaw.
* Do: "Level must be one of S1, S2, S3, S4, S5."
* Use one sentence pattern for every field, such as `<Field> must ...`, with the field name in the same form each time.
* Say the same kind of rule the same way. Don't write "1-40 characters" for one field and "at most 200 characters" for another.
* When several fields share a rule or a phrase, build it from one shared constant or helper instead of copying it. Keep `model` classes independent of `logic.Messages`.

* Share only text that means exactly the same for every field that uses it, and keep each field's own details in its own message. Don't merge messages just because they look alike. Each refactor counts against your freeze limit, so make it only where it fixes an inconsistency users can see.
* Before you change a message, read the messages for similar fields and match them, or change them together.
* When you change a message, update the tests that assert it and any UG text that quotes it. In the UG, describe the rule rather than quote the whole message.

* Tell format errors apart from invalid values. For a `YYYY-MM-DD` date, `2025-13-28` is a format error (the month must be 1 to 12), but `2025-02-30` is an invalid value (February has no 30th). Calling one the other is a bug. A combined "Invalid date or incorrect format" message is acceptable only if the team rules the distinction out of scope.
* Don't: use long keywords when short ones would do, case-sensitive keywords with no reason, or hard-to-type symbols.
* Don't: go so short that keywords become cryptic.
* Do: offer a short form and a descriptive form where it helps, the way `git commit -n` and `--no-verify` are the same.
### Match case sensitivity to the real world
* Names and search keywords are not case-sensitive in real life, so they must not be in the app.
* Don't: treat `filter n/alice` and `filter n/Alice` differently.

* `filter` replaces AB3's `find`. It combines different filters with AND. Text filters such as `n/` and `sch/` match any part of the value, ignoring case and extra spaces. Fields with fixed values, such as `lvl/`, `sub/`, `p/`, and `t/`, must match the whole value.
* The UG's `filter` section is the reference for this behavior. Keep the code and that section in sync.
* Don't: compare with exact string equality.
* Do: normalize before comparing (trim, collapse spaces, ignore case), as `Name` does for `Person.isSamePerson`.
* Do: when a match is likely but not certain, warn and let the user decide. `add` and `edit` ask for `CONFIRM` when only the name matches, and block a student whose name, school, and level all match.
* Do: state the detector's limits in the UG. Never imply that all duplicates are caught.
Support manual edits at least as well as AB3: a correctly edited file loads, and a wrongly edited one may be rejected but must not crash the app.
* Don't: switch to a format a person cannot reasonably edit by hand.
* Don't: promise more editing support in the UG than the app delivers.
* Do: when a field or the JSON format changes, make sure existing data files still load or fail clearly. Add valid, invalid, and old-format test files under `src/test/data`.
### Keep the UG and the app in sync
* A mismatch between the UG and the app is a bug, whichever side is wrong.
* Document every limit, restriction, and default that users can observe.
* Update the UG in the same PR as the behavior change.
* Make every feature easy to test. Each UG example must work when run in order on the sample data. A feature that testers can't easily try is a feature flaw.
* Don't: print stack traces, debug output, or alarming messages to the terminal during normal use.
* Do: log through `LogsCenter` at the right level. Do not use `System.out.println` for diagnostics.
### Do not hide behind "out of scope"
A missing or weak feature still counts as a flaw when:
* fixing it is essential for the app to be reasonably useful, or
* a clearly better behavior for the user would take little extra effort.
For every new or changed command, add tests for:
1. Plausible typing mistakes: missing space, missing or repeated prefix, extra whitespace, empty values, extra parameters, and text before the first prefix.
1. Case variants and realistic symbols, such as `s/o`, `-`, `'`, `+`, and `.`.
1. Boundaries: very long values, zero, negative numbers, and numbers too big for an `int`.
In each failure test, assert the exact error message and check that the model and data file are unchanged.
The [se-edu git conventions](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html) are graded, not optional.
* Subject line: imperative mood ("Add", not "Added"), capitalized, no trailing period. Aim for 50 characters or fewer; 72 is the hard limit.
* Optional scope prefix: `Person class: Remove static imports`.
* A body is optional. If you write one:
* Separate it from the subject with a blank line.
* Explain what changed and why, not how. Use bullet points if needed.
* Keep each commit to one logical change.
* Branch names are kebab-case. For issue work, use `<issue-number>-<keywords>`, for example `42-add-tag-command`.
Agents never change git history or the remote. The member commits and pushes, so RepoSense credits them.
* Do not run `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git merge`, `git rebase`, `gh issue create`, or `gh pr create`. Read-only commands such as `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log` are fine.
* When the work is done and [Before you push](#before-you-push) passes, end with commit instructions:

1. If the current branch is `master`, start with `git switch -c <issue-number>-<keywords>`. Changes never get committed to `master`. If no issue exists yet, draft its title for the member to create, as in step 1 of [Workflow](#workflow).
1. Split the changes into commits of one logical change each. Order them so every commit builds and passes tests on its own.
1. For each commit, give a `git add` command that lists exact paths and a `git commit` command with the full message. Never use `git add .` or `git add -A`.
1. If one file holds two logical changes, say so and tell the member to split it with `git add -p`.
1. During the feature freeze, report the `src/main` line count as described in [Current phase](#current-phase-feature-freeze-v16).
1. End with the `git push` command for the current branch.
1. If the branch is ready for a PR, draft the PR title and description as described in [Pull requests](#pull-requests).
git commit -m "Allow hyphens and apostrophes in names"
git commit -m "User Guide: Document allowed name characters" -m "Names can contain hyphens and apostrophes, but the User Guide
still says they must be alphanumeric."
RepoSense grades each member on the code they authored, so the human member is the only author.
* Do not add `Co-Authored-By:` trailers for AI tools to commits.
* Do not add AI tool links or "Generated with" lines to commits or PR descriptions.
These rules come from [Admin Appendix E](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/appendixE-gitHub.html). Grading scripts depend on them.
* Create each branch from the team repo's `master`, push it to your own fork, and open the PR from that branch. Never open a PR from `master`.
* Keep every branch after its PR merges. The scripts check that changes went through a branch.
* Update a branch by merging `master` into it. Never rebase or squash; both rewrite commit timestamps that the scripts use to track progress.

Every change to the team repo goes through an issue, a branch on the member's fork, and a reviewed PR. Source: [week 7 tP tasks](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/schedule/week7/project.html) and [Admin Appendix E](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/appendixE-gitHub.html).
Remotes: `upstream` is the team repo, and `origin` is the member's fork. Check with `git remote -v`.
1. Create an issue on the team repo for the task. Assign it to yourself, add `type.*` and `priority.*` labels, and set the milestone, such as `v1.1`.
1. Sync `master` with the team repo: `git switch master`, `git pull upstream master`, then `git push origin master`.
1. Create a branch from `master` named after the issue, such as `12-add-agent-instructions`. See [Branches](#branches).
1. Make the change with JUnit tests for the new or changed behavior, and update existing tests it affects. See [Tests](#tests).
1. Commit following the [Git conventions](#git-conventions), then push the branch to your fork: `git push origin <branch>`.
1. Before the last commit of the issue, check the whole branch for bugs it introduces, not just the latest change:
* Run `git fetch upstream`, then read `git diff $(git merge-base upstream/master HEAD)`. This covers every commit on the branch plus uncommitted changes.
* Check each change against [Preventing bugs and feature flaws](#preventing-bugs-and-feature-flaws) and the [test checklist](#test-checklist), and confirm the UG matches the new behavior.
* Report each bug with its file, line, and the input that triggers it. Fix it on the same branch before the PR is opened.
1. Open a PR from that branch to the team repo's `master`, following the rules below.
1. Get a teammate to review the PR. Resolve every comment before merging.
1. Close the issue, then repeat step 2 so your local repo and fork match the team repo.
At the end of each weekly milestone, right before the milestone is closed, check everything merged during it for bugs:
* Run `git fetch upstream` and list the merged PRs with `gh pr list --repo <team-repo> --state merged --search "milestone:<milestone>"`.

* Review their combined changes on `upstream/master`. Look for bugs that a single-PR check misses: features that conflict with each other, UG and app mismatches, and data files from the previous milestone that no longer load.
* Run the checks in [Before you push](#before-you-push) on an up-to-date `master`.

* Report each bug with its file, line, and the input that triggers it, and draft an issue title for the member to create. Close the milestone only after each bug is fixed or its issue moves to the next milestone.
Each member sends PRs for their own work, including their own part of the documentation. Do not commit a teammate's part for them.
* Keep each PR to one single, standalone, complete change: code, tests, UG, and DG together. Leave out unrelated changes.
* Title: when the PR fully fixes an issue, use the issue title. Otherwise, write it like a commit subject for the whole PR.
* Write `Fixes #123` for a full fix or `Fixes part of #123` for a partial fix.
* Keep it short, non-verbose and easy to read: one or two sentences on what changed and why, then a few plain bullets only if needed. The same applies to issue descriptions.
* Add before-and-after screenshots for UI changes.
* When drafting an issue or PR for the member, give the title and description as text they can paste into GitHub's web form.
* Assign the PR to the issue's milestone.
* Open the PR as a draft. Mark it ready for review only after CI passes and you have read the full diff for unintended changes.
* Never merge a PR while CI is failing.
* Use a merge commit. Do not squash or rebase.
* After merging, close the issue and sync `master` as in step 2 of [Workflow](#workflow).
Applies to `docs/` (User Guide, Developer Guide) and all Markdown in the repo.
* Use `*` for bullets, `_` for italics, and `1.` for every ordered list item.
* Put a blank line before lists, code blocks, and after headings. Put a space after `#`.
* Use second person ("you"), active voice, and present tense.
* Use American English spelling, such as "prioritize" and "color". Keep official names as written.
* Put code, commands, and file names in `code font`. Put UI elements in **bold**.
* Use the serial comma and descriptive link text (never "click here").
* When a feature changes user-visible behavior, update `docs/UserGuide.md` in the same PR.
* When a change affects design or architecture, update `docs/DeveloperGuide.md` and its diagrams in `docs/diagrams/`.

Graders and PE testers file bugs against text that is too long, unclear, or repeated. Source: [tP grading](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-grading.html) and [tP deliverables](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-deliverables.html).
* Use short sentences and plain words. Cut filler such as "note that", "simply", "in order to", and "please".
* Cut any sentence that does not help the reader use the app or understand the design. Cut repetition, not information: text that is too brief is also a bug.
* Say each fact once, where readers look for it first, and link to it from elsewhere. Watch for these repeats:
* Parameter rules restated in every command section.
* Error lists that restate a parameter rule.
* The same warning, tip, or note in several places.
* The same point made in both prose and a table.
* Keep the UG and DG consistent in terms: one name per concept, matching the glossary and the app.
* Use terms the reader knows. Define any other term in the glossary, or replace it with plain words.
* The UG must match the product exactly. Remove anything not implemented, or mark it **Coming soon**.
* Testers and graders read the UG and DG as web pages in current Chrome and Firefox, not as PDFs. Check layout and links on the rendered site, not only in the Markdown.
* Keep heading levels consistent so the table of contents is easy to navigate. Spell-check before you push; typos are bugs too.
* UG: open with the target user and the value proposition.
* UG: give each command a one-line purpose, its format, and one or two examples. Leave out detail that the error message already tells the user.
* UG: add a screenshot where it explains something words can't, such as the detail panel. Place it next to its text, and don't repeat near-identical screenshots.

* DG: write for a new team member learning the internal design. Keep what explains the design and cut low-level detail, such as exact message wording. Aim for comprehensible, not comprehensive. Use code snippets sparingly.
* User stories: each has all three parts (`As a ...`, `I can ...`, `So that ...`), the parts match, and no important story is missing.
* Use cases: steps are numbered correctly, each has the extensions it needs, and none mentions UI details such as colors or panels. Merge use cases that differ only slightly.
* NFRs: each is truly non-functional, measurable, and met by the product. Don't leave out a highly relevant one.
* Glossary: include every term the DG needs, and nothing it doesn't use.
* Manual testing: keep to the key cases.

* _Appendix: Effort_: write it. PE testers read it before estimating our implementation effort, which feeds the effort marks. In about one page, list the main implementation work beyond AB3 and what made each part hard. Don't overclaim; testers are told not to inflate estimates.
* Edit the `.puml` source in `docs/diagrams/` and regenerate its PNG in `docs/images/` with PlantUML. Never edit only the PNG.
* Use textbook UML notation exactly: line styles, arrowheads, multiplicities, and activation bars. A notation error is at least a `severity.Low` bug.

* Pick the diagram type for its purpose: class diagrams for structure, sequence diagrams for interactions, and activity diagrams for workflows. Use UML wherever it works as well as another kind of diagram.
* Keep architecture diagrams and their descriptions high level: components only, intuitive symbols, and no double-headed arrows.
* Make each diagram match the current code. Rename AB3 classes and methods, and delete diagrams, sources, and images that no page uses.
* A sequence diagram shows the internals of at most one component; treat other components as black boxes.
* Be consistent within and across diagrams, such as using activation bars everywhere or nowhere.
* If you leave out details on purpose, say so in a note.
* Keep diagram text about the size of the body text. Split a diagram that is too big to read.
* Match the patterns and style of the surrounding code. In this codebase, consistency matters more than cleverness.
* Change only what the task needs. Do not reformat, rename, or tidy other lines or files. Extra changes clutter the diff and credit the wrong member in RepoSense.

* Before you call a task done, run the checks in [Before you push](#before-you-push). Report the real result, including failures and their output. Never describe what the code should do in place of running it.
* Finish with the commit instructions described in [Commit handoff](#commit-handoff). Do not commit yourself.
* Add a line only if an agent would get it wrong without it. Do not restate what checkstyle, CI, or the linked guides already enforce.
* Add to an existing section. A new top-level section needs team agreement.
* For deep detail, link to `docs/` instead of copying it here.
* Edit through a PR that one other member reviews. Use subjects like `AGENTS.md: Add tag command conventions`.
* `CLAUDE.md` only imports this file. Put all content here.

This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
The `view INDEX` command passes the selected student from `Logic` to the student detail view without storing UI state in the `Model`.

The `view` command does not change the data being saved.

1. `Logic#execute` returns a `CommandResult` containing `DisplayMode.SHOW_STUDENT`, the selected `Person`, and the displayed index. An out-of-range index throws a `CommandException` instead, so `MainWindow` does not replace the current student detail view.
1. `MainWindow` reads the feedback, warning state, and cancellation notice from the result, then updates `ResultDisplay`.
1. `MainWindow#updateMainContent` reads the display mode, displayed index, and selected student from the result. It asks `Logic` for the current filtered list, which `Logic` obtains from `Model`.

The `StudentDetailPanel` places the student's details and notes in one vertical scroll pane. It listens to the filtered list and refreshes the record at the displayed index when that list changes. This allows edits to update an open student detail view while keeping the command's displayed index consistent with the list.

The app compares a student's normalized name, school, and level as the _student key_. Name comparison trims surrounding spaces, collapses repeated spaces, and ignores case. School comparison uses the same case- and space-insensitive behavior. Levels are compared by their `Level` values. The original text remains available for display. Phone, subject, and band do not contribute to the key.

`AddCommand` and `EditCommand` first reject a student key collision with command-specific error text, which `MainWindow` displays in red. The errors recommend adding a distinguishing identifier to the saved name (for example, `Chloe Tan 2`) when the records are different people; otherwise, identical name, school, and level values would make the students indistinguishable in the app. If only the normalized name matches, the commands request confirmation with command-specific prompt text, displayed in amber. Each matching school and level pair is separated by a semicolon so commas inside school names remain unambiguous. Each command also supplies an action-specific instruction on a separate line, followed by the shared cancellation guidance. On confirmation, they recheck the student key before changing the model. For an edit, the record being edited is excluded from both checks; edits that leave name, school, and level unchanged do not prompt. This prevents a prompt against itself or an unrelated phone, subject, or note change, and prevents a confirmed operation from bypassing the model's invariant.

The model enforces the student key through `UniquePersonList` for adds, replacements, and bulk resets. JSON loading uses the same check, so same-name records with different schools or levels load, while records with the same student key are rejected. `addnote` and `deletenote` replace a person without changing the key and remain valid. Delete and clear only remove records. Delete and delete-note prompts and feedback include school and level to distinguish same-name students. Sample data enters through the same model list and is subject to the same rule.
**Aspect: Which student records count as duplicates**
* Pros: Simple rule, simple model invariant, and a same-name record cannot be added accidentally.
* Cons: Blocks legitimate students who share a name, including siblings or students at different schools or levels. It provides no way to keep both records.
* Pros: Never blocks a legitimate enrollment, and the data model stays flexible.
* Cons: A repeated command can silently create indistinguishable records. Tutors can select or edit the wrong student, and the app offers no protection against accidental duplicate records.
* **Alternative 3 (chosen): Allow same-name records only when school or level differs; reject a repeated normalized name, school, and level.**

* Pros: Supports real students who share a name while blocking the most likely accidental repeat. A confirmation prompt handles uncertain same-name matches, and the hard model rule prevents a student key duplicate through add, edit, or data loading. The three fields are required for every student and together distinguish a student's current school-level record better than name alone.

* Cons: Two different students with the same name at the same school and level cannot both be entered under identical details, because TuteeBook would display them as indistinguishable records and the tutor could select or change the wrong one. The red add/edit error recommends assigning one a distinguishing saved name, such as `Chloe Tan 2`. A student moving to another school or level can be represented by an updated record, but the app does not retain two concurrent records with the same key. Name-only matching can also prompt for unrelated students.

The required subject and band are deliberately excluded from the key. A student can take several subjects and bands, and that list changes as lessons and courses change; using it would allow the same student to be added again merely by changing a subject or band. Subject-band details describe the student's studies, not who the student is. The phone is also excluded because it is optional, can change, and may be shared or unavailable.

Every student record must include a name, school, and level. Many tutors teach students with common names. School helps distinguish students who attend different schools. Level helps distinguish students at the same school who are in different levels. These fields block many accidental repeat entries while still allowing students with the same name when their school or level differs.

`Name` and `School` both use English letters and digits, so neither accepts other Unicode letters or numbers. A name starts with an English letter or digit and can contain only English letters, digits, and spaces; guardian names use the same rule. A school name must be 1 to 100 characters, contain at least one English letter, and can also contain spaces, periods, apostrophes, ampersands, parentheses, commas, and hyphens. Typed curly apostrophes are saved as `'`, but `School` still accepts `’` so that older data files load, and compares it as `'`, so `St. Joseph’s` and `St. Joseph's` are the same school in duplicate checks. Names and schools therefore share a letter and digit rule while retaining different punctuation rules for their fields. The parsers trim and collapse ordinary spaces before constructing these values. Direct model construction and JSON loading use the same validators.

The letter and digit rule also applies to existing data files. A file containing a name or school with any other letters or numbers fails validation when loaded, with the relevant field constraint. Users must edit those records in the previous version before upgrading. Previously supported school punctuation remains valid.

`Note` text uses the same English-letter approach, so an accented letter is rejected in a note just as it is in a name or school. A note can contain 1 to 500 English letters, digits, spaces, and keyboard symbols (together, the printable ASCII range `\x20` to `\x7E`), because notes record scores and reminders such as `WA2 Math: 36/50`. It also accepts the curly apostrophe `’`, as `School` does, so older data files with notes such as `Didn’t finish` still load. For any other character, `Note#getConstraintMessage` names the first one, and returns an emoji whole rather than half of its UTF-16 pair. `ParserUtil#parseNote` (used by `addnote` and `editnote`) and `JsonAdaptedNote` both use this message. `filter note/` search text is not restricted, like `n/` and `sch/` search text. A data file containing a note with any other character fails validation when loaded, so users must edit those notes in the previous version before upgrading.

`Address` accepts the same characters as `Note`, because addresses also need keyboard symbols such as `#`, `/`, and `,`, as in `Blk 123 Bedok North Ave 2, #04-111`. It declares its own copy of the allowed-character regex, as every field class owns its rules. `Address#getConstraintMessage` names the first character that isn't allowed, like `Note#getConstraintMessage`, and is used by the `Address` constructor, `ParserUtil#parseAddress` (used by `add` and `edit`), and `JsonAdaptedPerson`. Blank and too-long addresses keep the existing `Address.MESSAGE_CONSTRAINTS`. `filter a/` search text is not restricted. A data file containing an address with any other character fails validation when loaded, so users must edit those addresses in the previous version before upgrading.

`Address`, `Note`, `Phone`, and `Email` find the first character that isn't allowed with `StringUtil#findInvalidCharacter`, passing their own allowed-character regex. It returns an emoji whole rather than half of its UTF-16 pair.
**Aspect: Character rules for names and schools**
* **Alternative 1: Allow Unicode letters and digits in both fields.**
* Pros: Preserves names and school names in their original writing systems and supports accented spellings.

* Cons: Does not match the User Guide's definitions of English letters (`A`–`Z`, `a`–`z`) and digits (`0`–`9`). Names and schools would also continue to accept different character sets if their punctuation rules differ.
* **Alternative 2: Use the same strict English letters, digits, and spaces rule for both fields.**
* Pros: Gives both fields exactly the same simple validation rule.
* Cons: Rejects common official school-name punctuation such as periods, apostrophes, ampersands, parentheses, commas, and hyphens. Existing school records using that punctuation would fail to load.
* **Alternative 3 (chosen): Require English letters and digits in both fields, while retaining school-specific punctuation.**

* Pros: Rejects other letters consistently, preserves real school formats such as `Anglo-Chinese School (Independent)` and `St. Joseph's Institution`, and keeps parser, model, and storage validation aligned.

* Cons: Names and schools still have different punctuation rules, which must be documented. Accented letters and letters from other alphabets are rejected in either field, so existing records with them must be changed before upgrading.

The third option was selected because the issue was inconsistent handling of letters, not a need to make names and school names use identical punctuation. Allowing only English letters and digits rejects the accented school case consistently with student names, while keeping the punctuation needed for realistic school names. The User Guide lists the exact rules for each field and explains the existing-data limitation.

`ParserUtil#parseSchool` trims and collapses repeated spaces, then calls `School#getInvalidReason`, which returns a targeted message for the first problem found, in this order: blank input, more than 100 characters, the first unsupported character, then no English letter. `School#isValidSchool` uses the same checks, so `add`, `edit`, model construction, and JSON loading apply the same rules. The model and JSON adapter report the general `School.MESSAGE_CONSTRAINTS` instead of a targeted message.

Each student has 1 to 8 subjects. Every subject has a name and one band: `G1`, `G2`, or `G3`. Subject names can contain 1 to 40 English letters, spaces, hyphens, parentheses, commas, and ampersands, and must contain at least one letter. Digits, slashes, other letters, and other symbols are rejected. Subject names use English letters for the same reason as names and schools, as explained in [Student names and schools](#student-names-and-schools), so the same accented letter is handled the same way in every student field. A data file containing a subject name with any other letters fails validation when loaded, with the subject constraint. Users must edit those subjects in the previous version before upgrading. A student cannot have the same subject name more than once, even at different bands.

`Subject` is an immutable value object containing both the subject name and its required `Band`. The band is an enum, so a `Subject` cannot be constructed with an unsupported band or without one. For comparison, `Subject` trims surrounding spaces, collapses repeated ordinary spaces, and lowercases the name. The band is included in `Subject.equals`, but `Person#validateSubjects` checks names separately and rejects a repeated subject even if the bands differ.

1. `AddCommandParser` and `EditCommandParser` tokenize `sub/` and `band/`. `ArgumentMultimap#verifyEachFollowedBy` checks that each `sub/` is immediately followed by one `band/`. `add` requires at least one pair. For `edit`, giving neither prefix leaves the subjects unchanged; giving either prefix requires complete pairs and replaces the subject list.

1. `ParserUtil#parseSubjects` checks that the subject-name and band lists have the same number of values and that there are no more than eight pairs. It creates each `Subject` from the name and band at the same position, then calls `Person#validateSubjects` to reject repeated names.

1. `Band#fromString` converts the supplied value to the matching enum, ignoring case and surrounding spaces. `Subject` validates its name and requires a non-null band. These checks also apply when a subject is constructed outside the command parsers.

1. `JsonAdaptedSubject` stores a subject as a JSON object with `name` and `band` fields. During loading, it validates both fields and converts the band back to the enum. `Person` then validates the full subject list, so missing, invalid, or repeated subject data is rejected.

1. The student detail view and the result display show each subject with its band, such as `Mathematics (G1)`. `filter sub/Mathematics band/G1` matches a student only when that student has Mathematics at G1; omitting `band/` matches the subject at any band.
**Aspect: Whether to store a band for each subject**
* Pros: Keeps each subject entry simple and does not require the tutor to know or enter a band.
* Cons: The tutor cannot record or filter by the level at which a student takes each subject, even though students may take different subjects at different bands.
* **Alternative 2 (current choice): Store a subject and a required band together.**
* Pros: Every recorded subject has complete information. The model prevents a subject from existing without a valid band, and `filter` can match a subject at a specific band.
* Cons: The tutor cannot record a subject until they know its band.
* **Alternative 3: Store a subject with an optional band.**
* Pros: Allows the tutor to record a subject before its band is known.
* Cons: Adds a second state for every subject and requires commands, storage, and display to handle missing bands. Filtering by band must also distinguish between “any band” and “no band recorded.”

The app uses the second option because the tutor needs each subject’s band to plan lessons at the right level. Requiring it when the subject is entered keeps the model and stored data consistent. The pair format also makes the relationship explicit in commands: each `sub/` must be followed by its own `band/`.
**Aspect: Which characters to allow in subject names**
* **Alternative 1:** Keep the existing letters, spaces, and hyphens.
* Pros: Keeps validation simple and rejects punctuation that may be accidental.
* Cons: Rejects commonly used subject names such as `Science (Physics, Chemistry)` and `Design & Technology`.
* **Alternative 2 (current choice):** Also allow parentheses, commas, and ampersands.
* Pros: Accepts the real names reported in issue 263 while retaining the existing length limit and at-least-one-letter rule. Digits, slashes, and other symbols remain rejected.
* Cons: A subject can contain awkward punctuation placement because the rule checks allowed characters, not subject-name grammar.
* **Alternative 3:** Allow any printable punctuation and digits.
* Pros: Supports a wider range of current and future course names.
* Cons: Allows more accidental or inconsistent names than the issue requires, which can make subjects harder to recognize and filter consistently.

The app uses the second option because it resolves the reported real-name cases without making subject names unrestricted. The subject name remains one value before `band/`; the added characters do not change command tokenization.

`Address` is an optional value object. It accepts up to 200 English letters, digits, spaces, and keyboard symbols, as described in [Student names and schools](#student-names-and-schools), and collapses repeated ordinary spaces. It can't be blank. The add parser accepts optional `a/ADDRESS`; the edit parser replaces an address, and a blank `a/` removes it. `JsonAdaptedPerson` saves supplied addresses and accepts older JSON records without an address. The student list card shows an address when one is present; the student detail view and the result display show an em dash (`—`) when it is absent. Addresses do not contribute to duplicate detection.

`Email` is an optional value object that follows the same pattern as `Address`. `Email#isValidEmail` accepts a value of the form `local-part@domain` that is at most 254 characters, the longest address that SMTP allows (RFC 5321):
* The local part is groups of English letters and digits joined by single `+`, `_`, `.`, or `-` characters, so it cannot start or end with a symbol or contain two symbols in a row.
* The domain is labels joined by single periods. Each label is groups of letters and digits joined by single hyphens, and the last label has at least 2 characters.
* `ParserUtil#parseEmail` trims the value before validating it, so only a space inside the email is rejected.
`Email.MESSAGE_CONSTRAINTS` lists every rule in one message. Separate messages for each failure, such as a missing `@`, are left for a later version.

The add parser accepts optional `e/EMAIL`; the edit parser replaces an email, and a blank `e/` removes it. `JsonAdaptedPerson` leaves `email` out of the file when a student has none, and Jackson sets the field directly, so files without an email still load. Emails do not contribute to duplicate detection.

A domain with no period, such as `john@gmail`, is valid (`localhost` is a real domain) but is almost always a missing `.com`. Rejecting it would block valid addresses, so `AddCommand` and `EditCommand` save it and add a warning instead, the same way as for phones (see [Phone number validation](#phone-number-validation)). `Email#hasDotInDomain` does the check, and `Messages#getEmailNoDomainDotWarning` builds the warning. `EditCommand` only checks an email typed in that command.
A student has a set of `Tag`s, which may be empty but is never null. `Person#getTags()` returns an unmodifiable view that keeps the order the tags were typed in.

* A tag is one word of English letters and digits, where single hyphens may join parts of the word, such as `O-level`. `Tag` compares tags ignoring case, so `Exams` equals `exams`, and the display keeps the user's capitalization.

* `ParserUtil#parseTag` trims the value, then rejects a value containing a space with its own message, `Messages.MESSAGE_TAG_HAS_SPACE`, which tells the user to put `t/` before each tag (`filter` uses its own message, since it takes one tag). Other invalid values get `Tag.MESSAGE_CONSTRAINTS`. The space message lives in `Messages` because it names the `t/` prefix, which the model should not know about.

* `ParserUtil#parseTags` rejects a tag given twice with `Tag "X" is given more than once.`, instead of letting the set drop it silently. It takes plain strings, so the prefix handling stays in the parsers.
* In `add`, `t/` may repeat. In `edit`, the given tags replace all existing tags, and a single blank `t/` clears them. `EditCommandParser#parseTagsForEdit` handles both cases.

* `JsonAdaptedPerson` stores tags as a list of `JsonAdaptedTag` strings. Jackson sets the list directly, so files saved before tags existed load with no tags. A file with an invalid or repeated tag is rejected.
* Tags do not contribute to duplicate detection.

Tags are one word, so that they are quick to type and to filter by. Hyphens are allowed because realistic tags such as `O-level` and `N-level` contain them. This means `exam-prep` and `examprep` are different tags, which the User Guide states. Spaces are not allowed, because they would add a third spelling, `exam prep`, and because rejecting a space catches a common mistake: `t/paid urgent`, where the user forgot the second `t/`, is rejected with a message that explains how to give two tags, instead of being saved as one tag.
The tutor keeps notes on each student with `addnote`, `editnote`, and `deletenote`.
A `Person` holds its notes as an ordered `List<Note>`, and a `Note` holds only its text. A note's NID is its position in that list, so no ID is stored (see [Model component](#model-component)).

The note commands work like `edit`. Each command takes the student at the given index in the filtered list and copies their notes. It changes the copy, builds an edited student with `Person#copyWithNotes`, and replaces the student with `Model#setPerson`. The sequence diagram below shows `deletenote -f 1 nid/2`.
